<!-- Generated by scripts/gen-recipes.mjs from skills/hos/recipes/. Edit the recipes or recipe-pages/, not this file. -->

These recipes change hos itself. Your agent runs them against a checkout of the hos version you have installed, adds
a test, and opens a pull request to your fork. Ask: "Use the hos skill to …".

Each recipe declares the hos versions it fits (`hos:`) and the source files it relies on (`source:`); hos's own tests
fail when one of those files moves. This page is built from the recipe files, and each section's fold shows the
agent's part.

## Add a data source

Home has three sections: your tasks for today, a capture box and today's calendar. The Snags page lists snags. Each
one reads from a source. hos ships a local source, "This computer", for tasks, capture and snags. It has no calendar
source, so Home hides the calendar until you add one.

A data source plug-in is one small file in your brain's `hos/plugins/` folder. It reads from your own system: a task
app, a calendar, an issue tracker. It replaces the local source for its kind. A plug-in can also be a notifier: hos
hands it a short status screen (chats waiting for you, chats running, open snags) every minute and it sends that on.

hos runs plug-in code with its own rights. So whatever your approval settings say, hos asks you every time an agent
writes in `hos/plugins/` or changes the `plugins:` list.

**What you get:** a file in `hos/plugins/`, a line in `plugins:` in `hos/policy.yaml`, a Doctor row "Plug-in
&lt;name>", and your system's name on the Home section after a restart. hos itself doesn't change.

**Ask your agent:** "Use the hos skill to add a data source for &lt;my system>'s &lt;tasks / capture / calendar / snags>."

<details>
<summary>What the agent does</summary>

The full recipe is `skills/hos/recipes/add-a-data-source.md` in your brain (size M, for hos `>=0.1`).

**Ask the user (once, all together, defaults shown)**

1. **Kind**: `tasks` (Today list; hos also adds a task there when a hos task needs the user), `capture` (capture
   box), `calendar` (today's events, optional "now" line), `snags`, or `notifier`. One plug-in may provide several.
2. **How to reach the system**: a CLI on `PATH`, an HTTP API, or a local file. Where its credentials live: an
   environment variable or a config file outside the brain. Never in `hos/policy.yaml`, which the brain commits.
3. **A test backend** (a test list or project) for the write checks. Default: none, dry checks only.
4. **Plug-in name**: lowercase letters, digits and dashes, up to 41 characters. Default: `<system>-<kind>`.
5. **Options** it needs (a CLI path, a timeout). Default: none.

**Steps**

1. Read the interface in the hos checkout that matches `hos --version` (the `hos` key in `shared/LOCATIONS.md`, else
   ask): `src/plugins/types.ts` (the source interfaces and `PluginHost`), the kind table in
   `src/plugins/registry.ts` (required methods), and the checks for the kind in `src/plugins/kit.ts`. For snags,
   read `src/snags/README.md` too. Don't edit hos.
2. Draft the file in a scratch folder (the work folder), not in `hos/plugins/`, so each try doesn't raise an
   approval card. It is a plain ES module that imports nothing from hos; everything comes from `host`.

   ```js
   export default {
     name: 'my-tasks',
     apiVersion: 1, // 1 is enough for data sources; 2 adds host.acp and host.tools
     register(host) {
       const bin = typeof host.options.bin === 'string' ? host.options.bin : 'my-cli';
       host.provide({
         kind: 'tasks',
         version: 1,
         label: 'My app',
         async today() {
           // { available, tasks: [{ id, title, due: 'HH:MM' or null, link? }], error? }
           return { available: true, tasks: [] };
         },
         async done(id) { return { available: true, ok: true }; },
         async addLinked(title, priority, link) { return { ok: true, id: 'new-id' }; },
         async drop(id) { return { available: true, ok: true }; },
         async setPriority(id, priority) { return { available: true, ok: true }; },
       });
     },
   };
   ```

   Methods per kind (all async unless noted):
   - `tasks`: `today`, `done`, `addLinked`, `drop`, `setPriority`. Priority is `high`, `normal` or `low`.
   - `capture`: `capture(text)`, returns `{ available, ok, error? }`.
   - `calendar`: `today()` returns `{ available, events: [{ time, title }], error? }`. Optional `now()` (time
     blocks with `HH:MM` start and end) and `link` (an http(s) URL).
   - `snags`: `status()` (not async), `list`, `get`, `find`, `add`, `change`, `comment`, `localFile`. Keep files
     through `host.snagFiles`.
   - `notifier`: `push(screen)`; optional `everyMs` (default 60 s). Several notifiers may run.
3. Follow the host rules:
   - Call `host.provide()` only inside `register()`. Import and `register()` each get 10 s; do slow work inside the
     methods.
   - When the system can't be reached, return `available: false` with an `error`. Don't throw from a read.
   - Store state with `host.sqlite('<file>.db')`, which opens a file in the plug-in's own folder `host.dataDir`.
   - Use `host.now()`, `host.setTimeout()` and `host.log()`; use `host.fail(status, message)` for an error the API
     should show with that status.
4. Run the kit on the draft: `hos plugin-check <draft>.mjs --options '<json>'`. If the user gave a test backend, run it
   again with `--write`, which adds, changes and closes test items.
5. Copy the file to `hos/plugins/<name>.mjs` and add it to `hos/policy.yaml` (both raise an approval card):

   ```yaml
   plugins:  # plug-in files in hos/plugins/, loaded when hos starts
     - file: my-tasks.mjs
       options: { bin: my-cli }
   ```

   A plain `- my-tasks.mjs` line works when there are no options.
6. Ask the user before restarting hos, then run `hos keeper restart`. Plug-ins load only at start.

**Check**

```sh
hos plugin-check hos/plugins/<name>.mjs   # every line PASS, then "all checks passed"
hos validate                               # the plugins: list has the right shape
```

After the restart, the hos Doctor shows "Plug-in &lt;name>" as ok with "&lt;file> provides &lt;kinds>", and the Home section
shows the plug-in's `label`.

**If it fails**

The Doctor row and the kit say why. hos still starts without the plug-in.
- "plug-in files must sit in …": the file is outside `hos/plugins/`, or the list names another path.
- "is written for plug-in API N; this hos runs API M": lower `apiVersion`, or update hos.
- "… source "&lt;label>" is missing …": add the named methods.
- "did not finish register() within 10 s": move the slow work out of `register()`.
- "&lt;kind> already comes from the plug-in …": two plug-ins give the same kind; the first in the list wins. Remove one.
- Any throw in `register()` skips the whole plug-in. Fix it, run the kit, restart.

**Undo**

Remove the line from `plugins:` and restart: the local source comes back. Delete the file. Its data stays in the
plug-in's folder under the hos data dir. Tell the user it's there; don't delete it.

**Don't**

- Don't import from hos's `src/` or `dist/`. A plug-in that only uses `host` keeps working across hos versions.
- Don't put tokens or passwords in `options` or anywhere in the brain.
- Don't add code for a particular app to hos itself. Sources that are yours alone live in the brain.
- Don't run `--write` against the user's real lists.
- Don't restart hos without the user's yes in this chat.

</details>

## Add a harness

A harness is how hos runs one kind of coding agent. hos ships two: Claude, which runs the real Claude Code through
its Agent SDK, and a generic harness for any agent that speaks the Agent Client Protocol (ACP).

There are two ways to add an ACP agent, and neither changes hos:
- **No code:** a `harnesses:` entry in your brain's `hos/policy.yaml` with the agent's command, arguments and
  environment. This is the right way for most agents.
- **A plug-in:** a file in `hos/plugins/` for an agent that needs special handling (its own tool names, its own
  replay marker). hos asks you every time an agent writes that file or changes the `plugins:` list.

hos runs the agent's own program under your own sign-in. It never uses an API key and never stores the agent's login.

Some hos features need help from the agent. Each harness declares which ones it has, and hos hides the rest for its
chats: **Take over** (open the chat in a terminal), the **browser**, **context refresh** and **plan limits**.

**What you get:** the agent in the harness picker for new chats, a Doctor row for its sign-in, and its chats
surviving a restart. You need to restart hos once.

**Ask your agent:** "Use the hos skill to add &lt;agent> as a harness."

<details>
<summary>What the agent does</summary>

The full recipe is `skills/hos/recipes/add-a-harness.md` in your brain (size M, for hos `>=0.1`).

**Ask the user (once, all together, defaults shown)**

1. **The agent and its ACP command**, from its docs or `--help` (often `<agent> acp`). Check with `command -v` that
   it is installed. If it isn't, installing it is a `[user]` step. Don't install it yourself.
2. **id and label**: id is lowercase letters, digits and dashes, up to 40 characters. Chats store it, so never
   change it later. Default: the agent's name.
3. **Terminal, login and sign-in check commands**: the command that reopens a session in a terminal, with
   `{session}` where the session id goes (Take over), the login command, and a command that exits 0 when signed in.
   Default: none, so hos has no Take over for it and its Doctor row says "off".
4. **Models** (ids and the names of its model and effort options), **mode names** for build and plan, **memory
   files** it reads (for example `AGENTS.md`). Default: one model, "Agent default"; no modes or memory files.
5. **Slots** (its chats running at once; default 2) and **special handling** (default none, so path A).

**Steps**

1. Read the harness types in the hos checkout that matches `hos --version` (the `hos` key in
   `shared/LOCATIONS.md`, else ask): `src/harnesses/acp/config.ts` (`AcpConfig`, `AcpHooks`),
   `src/harnesses/acp/index.ts` (the `harnesses:` keys), `src/harnesses/harness.ts` (features).
2. **Path A, no code.** Add to `hos/policy.yaml`:

   ```yaml
   harnesses:  # ACP agents hos runs next to Claude; restart hos after a change
     - id: my-agent
       label: My agent
       command: my-agent
       args: [acp]
       terminal: [my-agent, --resume, '{session}']  # Take over; leave it out and hos hides Take over
       login: [my-agent, login]
       signed_in: [my-agent, whoami]               # exit 0 = signed in
       models: { default: fast, effort: high, list: [{ id: fast, label: Fast }] }
       model_option: model
       modes: { build: code, plan: plan }
       memory_files: [AGENTS.md]
   ```

   The other keys it takes: `env`, `pool`, `slots`, `effort_option`, `first_turn_note`, `aliases`. Any other key
   makes the entry fail. Effort is one of `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `max`.
3. **Path B, a plug-in.** Draft it in a scratch folder first, then copy it to `hos/plugins/<name>.mjs` (one approval
   card). It imports nothing from hos.

   ```js
   export default {
     name: 'my-agent',
     apiVersion: 2, // host.acp needs plug-in API 2
     register(host) {
       const command = typeof host.options.command === 'string' ? host.options.command : 'my-agent';
       const runtime = host.acp('my-agent', {
         name: 'My agent',
         command,
         args: ['acp'],
         terminal: [command, '--resume', '{session}'],
         login: [command, 'login'],
         signedIn: [command, 'whoami'],
         hooks: {}, // tool, replay, newSession, update, skills, autoAllow, serverReady
       });
       host.provide({
         kind: 'harness',
         version: 1,
         id: 'my-agent',
         label: 'My agent',
         models: () => ({ default: 'fast', effort: 'high', list: [{ id: 'fast', label: 'Fast' }] }),
         runtime,
       });
     },
   };
   ```

   Then add `- my-agent.mjs` to `plugins:` in `hos/policy.yaml`. Optional fields on the harness: `pool`, `slots`,
   `aliases` (old ids whose chats it should answer), `features`.
4. **Features.** An ACP harness has Take over when it names a `terminal` command; the rest are off. Set
   `features: { browser: true }` (or `contextRefresh`, `usageLimits`, `takeover`) only when the agent really does
   it. When one is off, hos answers Take over with "… has no Take over", hides the browser switch and refuses
   `browser: true` spawns, hides and refuses context refresh, and ignores its plan-limit events (so it can't slow
   Claude's chats).
5. **Tool names.** Approvals classify tools by the names in `host.tools` (`Read`, `Edit`, `Bash`, `WebFetch`,
   `Agent`, `mcp__<server>__<tool>` …). If the agent uses other names, map them in the `tool` hook. A name hos
   doesn't know is "unclassified" and asks by default.
6. Ask the user before restarting hos, then run `hos keeper restart`.

**Check**

```sh
hos validate                                # the harnesses: entry or plugins: line is valid
hos plugin-check hos/plugins/<name>.mjs     # path B: shape, features, sign-in
```

`hos plugin-check --write` starts the agent for one short turn. That uses the user's own subscription, so ask first.
After the restart: the agent is in the new-chat harness picker, and the Doctor shows "&lt;label> sign-in". Start one chat
on it, ask it to write a file, and approve the card.

**If it fails**

- Doctor row "Harness settings": the `harnesses:` entry names the bad key; fix it and restart.
- "… offers the harness id X, which … already uses": pick another id. Claude's id is taken.
- "&lt;label> sign-in" is down: the user runs the login command from the row in a terminal.
- A chat ends at once: run the ACP command by hand. Most often the agent isn't signed in or the arguments are wrong.

**Undo**

Remove the entry or the `plugins:` line and restart. Chats started on it stay in the store and answer "not
installed" until it comes back with the same id.

**Don't**

- Don't use an API key or copy the agent's login anywhere. The agent signs in by itself.
- Don't change an id once chats use it. Add the old id to `aliases` instead.
- Don't turn on a feature the agent lacks to make a button show.
- Don't write a non-ACP runtime here. That is a larger job: recipe `change-hos`, tested with `test/contract.ts`.

</details>

## Add a transport

hos listens only on this computer (loopback). A transport is how your other devices reach it: a service on this
computer publishes hos to your devices and tells hos who is asking. hos ships two, Tailscale and Cloudflare Tunnel
with Access. With none set, hos is reachable from this computer only.

A new transport is a change to hos's code, not a plug-in, because it decides who may use hos at all. Your agent makes
it in a new branch of your hos checkout, with tests, and opens a pull request to your fork (the recipe `change-hos`).

The transport must prove who is asking: a header that only the local service can set, or a token hos can verify.
hos's own passkey stays on top of it, so each new address needs its own passkey.

**What you get:** a pull request with the transport, its tests and its docs. After you merge it: a new value for
`transport:` in `hos/policy.yaml`, and a Doctor line that says whether it works.

**Ask your agent:** "Use the hos skill to add a transport for &lt;service>."

<details>
<summary>What the agent does</summary>

The full recipe is `skills/hos/recipes/add-a-transport.md` in your brain (size M, for hos `>=0.1`).

**Ask the user (once, all together, defaults shown)**

1. **The service**, and how it tells a local process who the visitor is: a header its local proxy sets, a signed
   token, a client certificate. If it can't prove the visitor, stop here: hos refuses transports without an
   identity check (ADR 0005).
2. **Name**: one lowercase word, used as `transport: <name>`.
3. **Settings it needs**, as keys under a `<name>:` block in `hos/policy.yaml` (for example a host name and the
   owner's account). Default: none.
4. **Previews**: should it also publish worktree dev servers? Default: no.

**Steps**

Run the recipe `change-hos` steps 1–4 first (pin the version, find the checkout, make a new worktree, read). Then:

1. Read `src/adapters/transport.ts` (the `Transport` interface), both transports beside it, ADR 0005, and
   `test/transport.test.ts`.
2. Write `src/adapters/<name>-transport.ts`, a class that implements `Transport`:
   - `name`: the word from answer 2.
   - `identify(req)`: return `{ user, via }` only when `fromLoopback(req)` is true (the request came through the
     local service) **and** the identity checks out against the configured owner. Return `null` otherwise.
   - `webOrigin(port)`: the https address the user opens, or `null` until it is known.
   - `previewUrl(port)`, and `previewPort(host)` if it publishes previews; `null` when it doesn't.
   - `doctor(port)`: `{ transport, ok, message, fix }`. One plain sentence, then the exact commands that fix it.
   - `codeViewHost()`: return what `loopbackTransport` returns, unless the service also publishes hos's terminal ports.
   - Put each outside call (a CLI, a key download) behind a small interface, the way `TailscaleCli` and
     `AccessCerts` are, so tests can pass a fake.
3. In `src/policy.ts`: add the name to `TRANSPORTS`, and write `load<Name>Config(file)` modelled on
   `loadCloudflareConfig`. It must throw a message that names the file and each missing key. Call it from
   `loaderErrors` in `src/cli/validate.ts`, next to the Cloudflare line, so `hos validate` reports it.
4. In `src/main.ts`: build the transport next to the other two. Add a flag (like `--tailscale-bin`) only for a path
   tests must point at a fake.
5. In `src/settings.ts`: add the `<name>` block to `CONNECTION` and `RESTART`, so Settings shows it under
   Connection and says it needs a restart.
6. In `schemas/policy.schema.json`: add the name to the `transport` list and describe the `<name>` block, so
   `hos validate` accepts it.
7. Tests at the daemon seam (ADR 0003), in `test/transport.test.ts`: add a fake identity to
   `src/fakes/fake-transport-identity.ts` and a `transport` option to `startTestDaemon` in `test/harness.ts`. Cover:
   - the owner's request is served;
   - no identity, another user, or a request not from loopback gets 401;
   - the doctor explains a broken setup without needing an identity;
   - a passkey is still required.
8. Optional live test: `test/<name>.live.test.ts`, skipped unless an environment variable is set, like
   `test/tailscale.live.test.ts`. Run it by hand only when the user asks.
9. Docs, in the same diff: the security page (`docs/site/src/content/docs/docs/security.md`) and the
   `set-up-phone-access` recipe if it lists the transports.

**Check**

```sh
npm run check -- transport policy settings
npm run test:full    # once, at the end, holding the hos-full-suite lock
```

Then hand over, as `[user]` steps: install and sign in to the service, set `transport: <name>` and its block, run
`npm run build && hos keeper restart` in the live checkout after the merge, open the new address and add a passkey
with the enrolment code hos prints at start.

**If it fails**

- 401 for the owner: `identify` reads the wrong header, or the request reaches hos through another hop, so it isn't
  from loopback. Print what the service actually sends in a test, not in the live daemon.
- hos exits at start with "transport must be one of …": the name isn't in `TRANSPORTS` in the build that runs.
- The passkey prompt fails on the new address: passkeys are per address. Enrol a new one there.

**Undo**

Before merge: close the PR and remove the worktree. After merge: the user removes `transport:` (hos goes back to
loopback only) and restarts.

**Don't**

- Don't make hos listen on anything but loopback. The service connects to hos locally.
- Don't trust an identity header on a request that didn't come from loopback.
- Don't skip or weaken the passkey. If the user insists, say so in the PR's first line.
- Don't install the service, open a tunnel or change machine settings. Those are `[user]` steps.
- Don't publish hos to the open internet without an identity check in front of it.

</details>

## Add a setting

A setting is a key in your brain's `hos/policy.yaml` that hos reads, such as `composer.paste_as_file_chars`. The
Settings page lists each one with the comment written next to it in the file.

To change a value, you edit the file. To make hos understand a new key, hos's code changes: it reads the key, checks
it, shows it in Settings, and the docs mention it. Your agent does this in a new branch of your hos checkout, with a
test, and opens a pull request to your fork (the recipe `change-hos`). Without the key, hos must behave exactly as it
did before.

**What you get:** a pull request. After you merge it and restart hos, you add one line to `hos/policy.yaml`.

**Ask your agent:** "Use the hos skill to add a setting for &lt;what it should change>."

<details>
<summary>What the agent does</summary>

The full recipe is `skills/hos/recipes/add-a-setting.md` in your brain (size S, for hos `>=0.1`).

**Ask the user (once, all together, defaults shown)**

1. **What it changes**, in one sentence. This becomes the comment on the key, which Settings shows.
2. **Key**: snake_case, at the top level or inside a block that exists (`composer.<key>`). Default: inside the block
   of the area it changes. Check that the name is free in `src/policy.ts` and the policy schema.
3. **Type, allowed values and default.** The default must be today's behaviour.
4. **When it applies**: on the next use (hos reads the file each time) or at start (needs a restart). Default: next
   use, when that is cheap.

**Steps**

Run the recipe `change-hos` steps 1–4 first (pin the version, find the checkout, make a new worktree, read). Then:

1. **Read it.** In `src/policy.ts`, add `load<Thing>(file)`, modelled on `loadComposer`: no file or no key returns a
   default constant; a wrong value throws `<file>: <key> must be …`.
2. **Use it.** Pass it from `src/daemon.ts`, where the policy file is already known as `file`.
   - Next use: hand over a function, as `composer: () => loadComposer(file)` does.
   - At start: read it once, and add the key to `RESTART` in `src/settings.ts`, so Settings marks it.
3. **Schema and validate.** Add the key with its type, range and a description to `schemas/policy.schema.json`. The
   schema refuses unknown keys, so `hos validate` says "unknown key" until this is done. Then add the new loader to
   `loaderErrors` in `src/cli/validate.ts`, so `hos validate` reports a bad value with the loader's own message.
4. **Settings.** `src/settings.ts` puts a key in a section by its top-level name: `models`, `composer`, `context`,
   `LIMITS`, `approvals` and `CONNECTION`. Any other top-level key shows under "Other". Add a new section only if the
   user asks.
5. **Comment.** Add the key to `test/fixtures/policy.yaml` with its comment on the same line, the way the other keys
   are written. That comment is the text Settings shows. Write the same line for the user to paste into their brain.
6. **A control in the app** (only if the setting needs one): every `<button>` and `<select>` in `web/src` needs a
   `title`, the hover text. `node scripts/check-hover-text.mjs` checks this.
7. **Tests** at the daemon seam (ADR 0003):
   - in `test/settings.test.ts`: `GET /api/settings` shows the key, its comment and, for a start-time key, its
     restart mark;
   - in the area's own test file: no key gives the old behaviour, a set key changes it, a bad value gives the clear
     error.
8. **Docs** in the same diff: one line on the docs page for that area (`docs/site/src/content/docs/docs/`).

**Check**

```sh
npm run check -- policy settings <area>
npm run check:e2e -- settings              # only if web/ or an HTTP route changed
npm run build && node dist/daemon/main.js validate --brain <temp brain with the key>
npm run test:full                          # once, at the end, holding the hos-full-suite lock
```

Build and validate in the worktree only, never in the checkout the daemon runs from.

**If it fails**

- `hos validate` says "unknown key": the schema step is missing, or the key is in the wrong block.
- The key doesn't show in Settings: the brain's file doesn't have it yet, or the key isn't under the top-level name
   that `src/settings.ts` reads.
- An existing test breaks: the default isn't today's behaviour. Fix the default, not the test.

**Undo**

Before merge: close the PR and remove the worktree. After merge: delete the line from `hos/policy.yaml`; hos goes back
to the default.

**Don't**

- Don't change what hos does for users who never set the key.
- Don't add a setting for a value nobody has asked to change.
- Don't put secrets in a setting. `hos/policy.yaml` is committed to the brain.
- Don't edit the user's own `hos/policy.yaml` as part of the code change. Hand them the line.

</details>

## Change hos

Fix a bug in hos or add a small feature, with your agent doing the work. It reads the docs and code of the hos
version you run, reproduces the bug first, changes the code, a test and the docs together, and opens a pull request
to your own fork. It works in a separate copy of the code, so the hos you are using keeps running.

It never merges, never restarts your hos and never touches your hos data. When the pull request is merged, you
rebuild and restart hos yourself (one line, below).

Use the brain recipes instead for changes to your own setup (approvals, actions, schedules, profiles). Those are
files in your brain, not hos code.

**What you get:** a branch and a pull request to your fork: the code, a test that failed before and passes now, and
the docs page that describes the behaviour.

**Ask your agent:** "Use the hos skill: hos does &lt;X> wrong" or "make hos do &lt;Y>."

<details>
<summary>What the agent does</summary>

The full recipe is `skills/hos/recipes/change-hos.md` in your brain (size M, for hos `>=0.1`).

**Ask the user (once, all together, defaults shown)**

1. **What is wrong or wanted**, with an example: what they did, what they saw, what they expected. A pasted error
   or Doctor row is enough.
2. **The hos checkout**: the `hos` key in `shared/LOCATIONS.md`. If it is missing, ask for the path. If there is no
   checkout, offer to clone their fork at the version `hos --version` prints, and add the `hos` row.
3. **Base branch**: default the checkout's default branch.
4. **A PR upstream too?** Default: no, only to their fork.

**Steps**

1. **Classify.** A question: answer from the docs page plus `file:line`, then stop. A config change: use the brain
   recipe for it and `hos validate`. A data source or harness from the brain: recipes `add-a-data-source`,
   `add-a-harness`. A transport or setting: recipes `add-a-transport`, `add-a-setting`, which return here. A bug or
   feature: go on.
2. **Pin.** Print `hos --version` (`hos <version> (<commit>)`) and the checkout's `git rev-parse --short HEAD` and
   `package.json` version. If they differ, say so and say which one the change targets. Default: the base branch,
   not the running commit, unless the user asks.
3. **Read**, in the checkout, in this order: `CLAUDE.md` (its rules win over this recipe), the docs in
   `docs/site/src/content/docs/`, the recipe's or page's `source:` files, `GLOSSARY.md`, the related `docs/adr/`,
   then search `src/` and `web/src/`. Write down `file:line` for the behaviour and for the test that covers it
   (`test/<area>.test.ts`, `e2e/<area>.spec.ts`).
4. **Worktree.** Make a new worktree on a branch `change-hos/<slug>`, never in the checkout the daemon runs from.
   Inside hos, use `workspace_create` with the repo and that branch (if the topic doesn't use the repo yet,
   `workspace_choose` lets the user pick it). Outside hos, use `git worktree add`. Then run `npm ci` in the worktree.
5. **Reproduce (bugs).** Make it fail first: a Vitest test at the daemon seam (ADR 0003), an e2e step, or a step on
   the throwaway daemon below. If you can't make it fail, report "not reproduced" with what you tried, and stop.
6. **Plan.** Anything bigger than one obvious line: list the files, the test and the docs page, then wait. Inside
   hos use `propose_plan`; outside, end the turn with the plan.
7. **Change** the code, the test and the docs page in the same diff, including any `source:` list that names a file
   you moved.
8. **Test**, tiered as `CLAUDE.md` says:
   - while working: `npm run check -- <areas>` (`--list` shows what it picks);
   - if `web/` or an HTTP route changed: `npm run check:e2e -- <areas>`, with a `HOS_E2E_PORT` no other worktree
     uses;
   - once, at the end: `npm run test:full`. Inside hos, hold the `hos-full-suite` lock (`lock`) while it runs.
     A test that passes only on retry is a snag: report it.
   - live tests only when the user asks: they spend the user's real subscription.
9. **Deliver.** Commit on the branch, push it to the user's `origin` (their fork), and open a PR to the fork's
   default branch with `gh pr create`. Offer an upstream PR only if answer 4 says so. If a snag started this, link
   it and resolve it with the commit once the user merges.

**Throwaway daemon** for a behaviour check, built from the worktree (`npm run build`), all data in temp folders:

```sh
T="$(mktemp -d)"; mkdir -p "$T/data" "$T/empty"
git init -q "$T/brain" && git -C "$T/brain" commit -q --allow-empty -m init
node dist/daemon/main.js --agent scripted --data-dir "$T/data" --brain "$T/brain" \
  --repo-root "$T/empty" --worktree-root "$T/empty" --tmux-socket "$T/tmux.sock" \
  --gh-bin test/fixtures/bin/fake-gh.mjs --port <free port>
```

`playwright.config.ts` starts hos the same way; copy any fake it sets. Open `http://localhost:<port>`, add a passkey
with the enrolment code it prints, and drive chats with the scripted commands (`write <name>`, `spawn &lt;role>
&lt;intent>`, `ask`, `plan &lt;title>`, `briefing` …, listed in `src/fakes/scripted-agent-runtime.ts`). Stop it with
Ctrl-C and delete `$T`.

**Check**

Report: the page and sentence that describe the behaviour, the files changed, the test that went from failing to
passing, the check results, and the PR link. Then the line for the user: "To run it: merge, then
`npm run build && hos keeper restart` in your hos checkout."

**If it fails**

- `npm run check` picks no test for a file: pass area names (`npm run check -- <area>`).
- The full suite waits: another worktree holds `hos-full-suite`. Wait; don't take it from them.
- The change needs a new config key: that's recipe `add-a-setting`.

**Undo**

Close the PR and delete the branch and the worktree. Nothing else changed.

**Don't**

- Don't write under the hos data dir (`--data-dir`, default `~/.hos`: the database, push keys, passkeys, enrolment
  code, backups, the Config vault). Read it only through the HTTP API or the Doctor.
- Don't read, print, move or create secrets: Keychain items, sign-in tokens, the brain's `scripts/secret.sh` values,
  `.env*` files.
- Don't restart, stop or rebuild the running daemon, or run `npm run build` in the live checkout, without the user's
  yes in this chat.
- Don't push to any `main` or default branch, force-push, `npm publish`, tag a release or merge your own PR.
- Don't install software or change machine settings (launchd, systemd, Tailscale, Cloudflare, `pmset`). List them as
  `[user]` steps.
- Don't let tests touch the user's real repos, tmux server, Keychain or subscriptions: temp folders, a separate tmux
  socket and the injected fakes only.
- Don't edit the brain's `hos/*.yaml` or profiles as part of a code change. That is a separate brain edit.
- Don't weaken a safety default (approvals, loopback-only, passkeys, the kill switch) without saying so in the PR's
  first line.

</details>

## Plug-ins from your brain

Things that are yours alone, such as a data source for your own task app or an agent that needs special handling,
can live as plug-in files in your brain's `hos/plugins/` folder, listed under `plugins:` in `hos/policy.yaml`. hos
loads them at start. Each plug-in registers what it provides through one small, versioned interface per kind, so a
plug-in written today keeps working. Because the server runs this code with its own rights, your policy can make hos
ask you every time an agent changes a plug-in file or the `plugins:` list (`approvals.plugin_edits: ask_every_time`;
the starter brain sets it).
